#4461. Ford’s EV batteries retain more than 90% health after 100,000 miles

Your electric vehicle battery may last longer than you think. Ford says its EV batteries retain greater than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. Here are a few tips to keep yours healthy.

The Mustang Mach-E went on sale in late 2020 as Ford’s first fully electric crossover SUV designed from the ground up.

Since launching the 2021 Mustang Mach-E, Ford has been collecting data from over 36,000 vehicles that have traveled two billion miles across the US and Canada.

According to Ford, the Mach-E’s battery has retained 92% of its health on average over the past five years.

Across its full EV lineup, including the F-150 Lightning and E-Transit, Ford said its battery packs maintain more than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. The key number to look at is the spread, with 95% of vehicles falling between 87% and 97% health.

Of 2021 model-year EV owners, Ford said, more than 2,000 have crossed 100,000 miles with their original battery averaging better than 91% health, while over 30 have crossed the 200,000-mile mark and average 88% health.

Ford is using real-world data to help owners take good care of their electric vehicles, no matter how much they know about batteries and other EV tech.

It’s also applying lessons from developing the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, which will underpin its next-generation EVs, starting with the Fantom pickup next year.

Ford offered a few simple, everyday tips to help owners support long-term battery health. For one, if possible, charge at home on Level 2 for daily commuting or driving and save DC fast charging for longer trips.

It also helps to avoid charging in extreme temperatures if you can. Preconditioning the battery can help bring it into the optimal temperature range, while parking in the shade on hot summer days can also help avoid long-term battery degradation.

Last, but not least, you can use the Ford App to find charge-level recommendations designed specifically for your vehicle and battery system.

The 2021 Mustang Mach-E uses an NCM battery, but some newer Ford batteries use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry, which is recommended to charge to 100% from time to time.

Ford has introduced new features in the Ford App to help owners maintain battery health specific to their vehicle and will continue to use the data to improve the experience as it introduces its next-gen EVs.

Important to recognize that assessing long-term battery health is like looking into outer space, in that the info you're receiving is already out of date. Battery management systems are improving all the time, and more durable chemistries are being released.

Ford will open pre-orders for the Fathom, a midsize electric pickup and first UEV-based model, starting at $28,350 in early 2027.

Meanwhile, the 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E is now on sale, starting at $39,995. The 2027 Mach-E drops the standard-range battery offered in the 2026 model and now comes standard with the larger 88 kWh battery with an EPA-estimated range of up to 320 miles (RWD).

Want to take a closer look at one for yourself? You can find available Ford Mustang Mach-Es around you and see local offers here using our partner link.

#4460. The electric Vespa just got better where it actually matters

Vespa’s electric scooters have never exactly screamed for attention. That’s sort of the point. They look like Vespas, ride like Vespas, and just happen to swap the gasoline engine for a much quieter electric drivetrain.

But for 2027, Vespa has given its electric lineup a fairly significant technological overhaul while leaving that iconic steel bodywork largely untouched.

Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new electric Vespa lineup now consists of the Primavera Elettrica, Sprint S Elettrica, and the faster Primavera Tech Elettrica. And while you’d be forgiven for struggling to spot the differences from across the show floor, there’s a lot more happening underneath.

The biggest upgrade is an entirely new electric motor developed and manufactured in Italy by Vespa parent company Piaggio Group. The motor uses a new modular design intended to improve both performance and efficiency, while also doing away with rare-earth materials.

On the 45 km/h (28 mph) Primavera and Sprint S models, Vespa says the new motor provides stronger acceleration for stop-and-go city riding. Range reaches up to 85 km (53 miles) in Eco mode.

But perhaps the biggest practical improvement is the new removable battery. Being able to pull the battery out of the scooter and carry it inside for charging makes a massive difference for urban riders who don’t have access to a garage or dedicated charging spot – exactly the kind of riders Vespa is targeting.

The Primavera Tech is where things get a little faster. This version is homologated as a motorcycle rather than a moped in Europe and reaches 67 km/h (42 mph). That’s still not terribly fast, but the electric Vespa line has never been known for its top speed.

Its range has increased by 12.5% thanks to the new motor and Vehicle Management System, reaching 90 km (56 miles) on the WMTC cycle or up to 100 km (62 miles) in Eco mode.

There’s also a new charger that Vespa says reduces energy consumption from the wall by 17%, with a 0-80% charge taking around 2.5 hours. A new Maintenance mode is designed to protect the battery during longer periods when the scooter isn’t being ridden.

Nice. I've always liked the idea of Vespas. My riding requires something a bit bigger, but they're cute as a button.

The Primavera Tech also gets the technological bells and whistles you’d expect from the flagship version, including a 5-inch TFT display, keyless operation, navigation through Vespa’s smartphone connectivity system, and remote seat unlocking.

Perhaps the most Vespa thing about the whole update is how little of it you can actually see.

The company hasn’t tried to turn its electric scooters into rolling science-fiction props. They’re still unmistakably Vespas, complete with the same classic styling that has defined the brand for generations. They just happen to have a much more interesting electric drivetrain hiding underneath now.

Of course, they also carry some very Vespa pricing. While we don’t have word on the updated pricing for the new models, the outgoing Primavera Elettrica 70 RED was priced at $8,299 in the US. So don’t expect these models to come cheap.

#4459. Ezra Dyer: Maybe the Saturn Sky Red Line Is Not Quite a Discount Viper, but It Comes Close

This car is proof that the old GM’s ideas weren’t all bad, as I find out when I take custody of one.

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

Back in 2007, I gave my father-in-law, Roger, a ride in a Dodge Viper test car. He loved it, and I offhandedly said, “If you like this, a Saturn Sky Red Line is 80 percent of the performance for 30 percent of the price.” That was the extent of my salesmanship, so I was surprised a month or so later to learn that he’d gone out and bought a new Sky Red Line—for less than $30,000.

I mean, people ask me for car-buying advice all the time. But the way it usually works is that someone asks my pick for an electric sedan, I tell them to drive a Lucid Air, and then they buy an F-350 Power Stroke. So Roger’s follow-through was both rewarding and unnerving, because now he owned a Sky, and I owned my opinion, which is dangerous. I once had a boss who asked me to name a car that was “overpowered but understated,” and I blurted three words that I came to regret: “Volkswagen Phaeton W-12.” I think soon thereafter the company handbook was amended to make Phaeton recommendations a fireable HR violation.

See all results for used cars for sale near 80203

Fortunately, Roger liked the Sky, the first new GM car he’d purchased since a 1982 Camaro Berlinetta that was so terrible that he swore he’d never buy another GM vehicle. He usually sticks to such decrees, but maybe Saturn got a pass because the brand wasn’t around when his Chevy was putting him on a first-name basis with the local tow-truck dispatchers. In any case, the only problem the Sky ever had pertained to the notorious GM ignition-switch recall, wherein pre-bankruptcy GM’s pathological commitment to cheapness led to ignition cylinders unfit for a Little Tikes Cozy Coupe and thus occasional random engine shutdowns. This happened to Roger once on a back road, but he was unbothered. “I just put it in neutral, restarted it, and kept driving,” he told me. “Didn’t even stop.” I guess the Camaro might have permanently recalibrated his expectations for build quality.

Eventually, Roger stopped driving, but he still liked the Sky, so it sat in his driveway long enough for the neighbors to plant hedges so they wouldn’t have to look at it. But where they saw a dented, pollen-crusted car with two flat tires, I saw a dented, pollen-crusted car with two flat tires and a 260-hp turbo four, a stick shift, rear-wheel drive, and a limited-slip differential. Roger said that if I could get it going, I could have it for the bargain price of “get it out of my driveway.”

So, one day, I arrived with a battery jump pack, an air compressor, and five gallons of fresh gas. The questionable tires held air, and the electrics powered up. I splashed in some fuel and turned the key. The Sky fired up like it had been parked an hour before, its digital odometer showing just 43,000 miles. I put it in neutral, let out the clutch, and it immediately stalled because it wasn’t actually in neutral. Turns out you can wiggle the Red Line shifter side to side quite a bit even when it’s in second gear.

See all results for used cars for sale near 80203

Other revelations mostly pertained to ran-when-parked status. The flat-spotted tires and various wheel-on-curb encounters gave the Sky the ride and directional stability of a grocery cart you pull out of the corral and immediately swap for a different one. The battery wouldn’t hold a charge, the interior smelled like a cologne called Old Must, and the A/C didn’t blow cold. But the scrappy Red Line ran like a champ, the turbo issuing a jaunty chirp on upshifts and all 260 horses feeling ready to gallop. It just needed a little deferred maintenance.

I bought some Pirelli P Zeros and got an alignment, since I’ve found that cars drive better with round tires all pointed in the same direction. I changed the oil and recharged the A/C. Next, I tackled the battery, which is mounted somewhere near Earth’s molten core. Accessing it requires removing the right front fender, and I got impatient and only mostly unbolted it, figuring I could bend the flexible composite panel enough to get the battery out. That’s how I tore a fender while replacing the battery, which is not a sequence of words I expected to write back when I told Roger that a Sky Red Line is a discount Viper.

But I stand by my assessment. The Sky was, and is, huge fun. It’s agile and powerful, low-slung and eager to carve a corner. It makes any drive feel like Bowser and Koopa Troopa should be trying to beat you to the finish line of Rainbow Road. The critiques that dogged the Sky when it was new—cheap interior, little storage space, poor visibility—seem less important now. Saturn ran out of time to perfect the Sky, but it’s perfect enough. Dents and all.

Ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive.

#4456. Toyota sells 3 electric SUVs, but which one is best for you?

Toyota now offers three fully electric SUVs: the bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland. Here’s how they stack up.

After introducing the new and improved bZ (formerly the bZ4X) in late 2025, the electric SUV quickly became one of the most popular EVs in the US.

In the first nine months of 2026, it was the fourth-best-selling electric vehicle, behind the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

With two additional electric SUVs now on sale, the CH-R and bZ Woodland, Toyota has suddenly become one of America’s top-selling EV brands.

Its EV sales have nearly tripled this year. According to Cox Automotive, Toyota ranked as the third most popular EV brand behind Tesla and Rivian in the third quarter.

Toyota offers three distinct electric vehicles: the 2027 bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland, each designed for different lifestyles, so which one is the best fit for you?

After launching the updated model last year, the 2027 bZ starts at $34,980. With the $1,595 delivery fee, the starting price is $36,576.

That’s for the standard 2027 Toyota bZ XLE FWD with an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 236 miles. For longer range, you can upgrade to the FWD Plus model, which offers up to 314 miles and starts at $37,980 (excluding the delivery fee).

The Toyota bZ is available in XLE and Limited grades, with front- or all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrains.

Two battery options are offered: The 57.7 kWh battery on the standard XLE FWD provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 236 miles, while the larger 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 288 miles of range on the XLE AWD and 314 miles on the XLE FWD Plus model.

FWD models produce either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models deliver a combined 338 hp.

The 2027 bZ also has a built-in NACS port, so you can use Tesla Superchargers without needing a separate adapter. Toyota said it takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.

Inside, the 2027 bZ features Toyota’s updated cabin design. The setup features a 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and a new 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The bZ is essentially designed as an everyday driver with a long driving range, modern tech, and available AWD.

For those looking for a bigger, more rugged option, the 2027 bZ Woodland may be a better fit. The Woodland is 6″ longer than the standard bZ and comes with standard AWD.

The longer body opens up more interior space, with up to 74.3 cubic feet of storage compared to the bZ with up to 67.1 cubic feet.

Unlike the bZ, the Woodland model has a standard AWD powertrain with Toyota’s X-Mode control system.

The setup delivers a combined 375 horsepower, 37 hp more than the standard bZ, making it Toyota’s most powerful EV currently.

It also adopts a more commanding, upright stance with 8.3″ of ground clearance and 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.

Although it uses the same 74.7 kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland’s EPA-estimated range drops to 281 miles because of the added weight and power. Upgrading to the optional all-terrain tires sacrifices even more range, with up to 260 miles.

Like the bZ, the Woodland also has a built- in NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes around 30 minutes.

Inside, the bZ Woodland features the same 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380. All variants include standard roof rails, Dual Qi-capable wireless device chargers, heated front seats and steering wheel, and Digital Key capabilities.

Last, but not least, the C-HR is a smaller, sporty, coupe-like electric SUV. The 2027 Toyota C-HR starts at $37,080, or $2,100 more than the standard bZ.

It’s about 6.7″ shorter than the bZ, with a smaller wheelbase, but also comes with standard AWD. The dual-motor AWD setup delivers a combined 338 hp, not quite as much as the bigger, more powerful Woodland.

The C-HR is available exclusively with the 74.7 kWh battery, which provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 287 miles for the SE grade with 18″ wheels.

Upgrading to 20″ wheels adds a street-ready look but offers slightly less EPA range, with up to 273 miles.

The coupe-like design adds a sleek look and opens up interior space, with up to 59.5 cubic feet of rear cargo space when the rear seats are folded. That’s slightly more than the bZ, which offers up to 56.9 cubic feet.

Inside, the C-HR features the same setup as its other EVs, including a 7″ slim driver’s display and 14″ central infotainment screen.

Like Toyota’s other electric SUVs, the C-HR has a native NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes about 30 minutes.

These are all basically the same small vehicles. I did not fit in any of them (6’ 2”) it is so frustrating to have less than 300 miles of range on AWD versions that are supposed to be better models.

It is 2026 over a decade since EVs arrived and over 5 years after the Tesla Model Y with practically zero competition almost at same price (Rivian R2 may be next year when affordable versions ship.) BMW, Mercedes and Volvo need $10k more. Hyundai has kept EV5 out of USA.

It is almost like none of the Legacy automakers want any SUV that can compete on price.

The 2027 Toyota C-HR EV is available in two trims: SE and XSE. Standard features include two wireless Qi phone chargers, low-profile roof rails, Fabric/SofTex-trimmed seating, heated front seats and steering wheel, Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, and a power liftgate.

Which Toyota electric SUV would you choose? The bZ, C-HR, or bZ Woodland? Or would you choose another EV? Let us know your pick in the comments. Next year, Toyota will add the Highland EV, its first three-row electric SUV.

#4455. 10 Abilities That Ruin Good Pokémon

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

There are some amazing Pokémon out there that are great for both playing through the game and using them in competitive battles. These Pokémon are often the go-to for those who like to play competitively.

However, there are also Pokémon that are good, but they are absolutely ruined because they have a bad ability. Think of Pokémon like Slaking, who has a high base stat total, but the fact that it has the Truant ability makes it so it can only attack every other turn.

Otherwise, this Pokémon is just loafing around. There are several Pokémon like this that would be amazing if it wasn’t for a terrible ability holding it back.

Swampert is a great Pokémon, and one my go-to starter Pokémon line in Ruby and Sapphire. It has solid stats, with it being a good attacker who only gets better when it Mega Evolves.

The only thing lacking for Swampert is its speed, as it only has 60 speed, but the rest of its stats more than make up for its lack of quickness. Unfortunately, it has two abilities that somewhat ruin it. These abilities are Torrent and Damp.

Damp just prevents explosions, and Torrent increases Swampert’s water-type moves, but only when it is low in health. Thankfully, Mega Swampert gets Swift Swim, which doubles its speed in the rain.

I mentioned it in the intro, but it needed to be an entry on this list, because Slaking is one of the all time greatest Pokémon stats-wise, but its ability makes it so it can’t do anything.

If you weren’t aware, Slaking has a base stat total of 670, which means that it rivals legendary Pokémon like Rayquaza. With power like that, Nintendo and Game Freak needed a way to make it so Slaking didn’t destroy the world, so they gave it Truant.

Truant makes it so it has to loaf around every other turn, leaving it open to attack and set-up moves. This ability absolutely destroys Slaking, making it a complete pass in most circumstances.

Regigigas is a powerhouse, and there is no denying it. With an attack stat of 160, this Pokémon dominates with physical attacks. However, it is ruined by its horrible ability, Slow Start.

Slow Start may sound like it simply slows a Pokémon down, and that is partly true, but it is worse than that. This ability makes it so the Pokémon’s speed and attack stats are both halved for the first five turns of battle.

Five turns is a ridiculously long time to have half of your attack, and it basically ruins Regigigas, as it can be defeated within those first five turns by any competent trainer. Just bring out a special attacker, and Regigigas doesn’t stand much of a chance.

A complementary Ability can turn a weak, stat-challenged Pokemon into a force to be reckoned with and here are the best.

Machamp is a fan-favorite Pokémon that is an absolute powerhouse. It rocks an overall base stat total of 505, with a high attack stat, decent defense, and decent HP. Unfortunately, it is brought down by the ability No Guard.

No Guard was the signature ability of the Machamp line prior to Generation V, and it makes it so enemy and player attacks always land. This means that accuracy suddenly doesn’t matter as both Pokémon will always hit their target.

This means that even 1-hit KO moves are guaranteed to land, and if Machamp is outsped, then it is curtains for this Pokémon. It doesn’t help too much that Machamp also has Guts, which increases its attack by 50%, but only when it has a status condition.

To be fair, Illuminate isn’t the worst ability out there, but it has absolutely no effect in battle, making it completely useless to have on a strong Pokémon. Starmie is one such Pokémon that has a useless ability.

Instead of Illuminate affecting anything in battle, it simply increases your encounter rate outside of battle. This is okay whenever you are trying to farm for a specific Pokémon, but it is otherwise useless.

It would be nice for this to be a hidden ability on Starmie instead of its primary ability alongside Natural Cure (which has a little more value). Thankfully, it gets the ability Huge Power whenever it Mega Evolves, as this amplifies its power.

Imagine that you caught a Wimpod. You stuck with it despite its flaws, raised it to level 30, and you were rewarded with it evolving into Golisopod. This is a significant power boost. After all, it has a base stat total of 530.

Unfortunately, the ability Wimp Out, which is the main ability of Wimpod, has changed into Emergency Exit. While the name of the ability has changed, the effect of the ability has not, making it so Golisopod will switch out whenever its health falls below 50%.

This ability isn’t the worst, but it does make using Golisopod a bit of a nuisance. After all, it may be a great match-up against a Pokémon you are fighting, but then it switches out because its health got too low.

From Ultra Necrozma’s stat boosts to Volo’s grueling final battle, these Pokémon encounters bend the rules to deliver memorable challenges.

Gallade is a great Pokémon that matches the 518 base stat total of Gardevoir, is psychic and fighting type, and hits like a truck with its 125 attack stat. However, the ability Steadfast is pretty pointless.

Steadfast is an ability that increases the Pokémon’s speed by one stage whenever it flinches. This is an okay ability, but it doesn’t come into effect very much, which is unfortunate since Gallade doesn’t have the best speed.

It has an 80 speed stat, which means there are a lot of Pokémon that will outspeed it. However, they have to specifically use flinching moves to make Gallade’s speed increase, and if that doesn’t happen, then the ability never gets used, making it a complete waste.

Rhyperior is a hefty Pokémon with a base stat total of 535, making it very powerful, especially with an attack stat of 140. It also boasts high defense, with a score of 130, and great health that has a score of 115. It is a tank, and it needs to be since its speed stat is only 40.

However, the worst part about Rhyperior is the ability Lightning Rod. This ability makes it so any single-target eclectic attacks are redirected to Rhyperior. Since Rhyperior is a ground-type it isn’t affected by electric attacks.

However, the only way this ability is effective is if you are doing double-battles. After all, nobody would dare bring out an electric-type Pokémon against a ground type, unless the sprinklers are on. Solid Rock does help its defences, but with those pesky x4 weaknesses, it's not going to do enough.

Archeops is coming in with a staggering 567 base stat total. This is very impressive, especially when you look at its attack and speed stats, which happen to be 140 and 110. It hits fast, and it hits hard.

Unfortunately, Archeops is a bit of a Defeatist, and by that, I mean it has the ability Defeatist. This horrible ability makes it so that the Pokémon’s attack and special attack are halved whenever its health falls below 50%.

One solid hit on Archeops that takes it below 50% health, and suddenly its attack is heavily nerfed. It wouldn’t be so bad if it could fall back on its special attack, but that is also halved.

Camerupt is a solid Pokémon with a base stat total of 460. This isn’t as strong as some of the other Pokémon on the list, but it is up there. It has both a solid special attack and attack, with them being 105 and 100.

As is the case with every Pokémon on this list, it has an ability that is pretty much useless. It gets Magma Armor, which prevents the Pokémon from becoming frozen. While this sounds good, you have to think that Camerupt is a fire type Pokémon.

If you know type effectiveness, then you know that fire-type Pokémon are super effective against ice types. In other words, nobody would dare use an ice-type move against Camerupt, even if it doesn't resist it because of its secondary ground typing. Solid Rock serves it better, though again its 4x weakness to water will usually be too much with or without it.

This list includes some Pokémon that are stronger than their evolutionary forms.

#4454. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

#4453. Track Attack: We Drive the 2028 Audi Nuvolari to the Limit

Unfamiliar surroundings can elicit feelings of uneasiness. We’re in Madrid; we’ve just rolled out of bed and arrived at Circuito de Madrid Jarama. A few minutes pass, and we’re belted into the passenger seat of the Audi’s newest halo car, the Audi Nuvolari, itself a relatively unexplored place. Site laps are sometimes easy, but not today. Our tour guide, Victor, has a crazy look in his eye. And maybe a screw loose. He attacks the braking zones, exits corners sideways, and shows zero restraint in his speed. Victor, we love you, but can you save a little tire for the rest of us?

We enjoyed our first experience with Audi’s first mid-engine car since the dearly departed R8. After just three laps driving around the former home of the Spanish Grand Prix, we love the Nuvolari. Having spent time with the Nuvolari’s donor plug-in hybrid platform, the Lamborghini Temerario, eases the tension.

The Audi’s cabin, a cocoon of microfiber and leather with aluminum door handles, seat controls, and vents, oozes fancy-dinner vibes more so than qualifying laps. It’s a welcoming environment. Strapped into the driver’s seat, the Nuvolari starts up in its pure electric mode. Turning the top-left knob on the busy steering wheel wakes the 789-hp twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8; its flat-plane crankshaft is capable of spinning to a bonkers 10,000 rpm. The cabin fills with glorious noise, most of it real. Turning and holding that same knob activates Dynamic+ mode, summons more noise, and puts most of the systems in their most-ready state.

See all results for new 2028 Audi Nuvolari for sale near 22206

Exiting Jarama’s final corner and pointing down the straight, the Nuvolari accelerates as if it were shot off an aircraft carrier’s flight deck. As in the Temerario, the screaming V-8 has friends. A 147-hp motor connected to the crankshaft fills the lulls in the engine’s torque delivery. The front axle has two 147-hp motors that also provide torque vectoring. While the Temerario stores its energy in a 4-kWh battery, the Nuvolari (like the new Lamborghini Revuelto SV) utilizes a larger 7-kWh pack. The new pack supplies up to 254 horses, compared to the Temerario’s 187-hp limit. In all, the V-8 and electric motors work together to create a 987-hp party, or 80 more than the Temerario.

By the end of Jarama’s nearly half-mile front straight, we’ve almost reached an indicated 185 mph. The Nuvolari brakes as effortlessly as it accelerates, courtesy of Brembo CCM-R Plus carbon-ceramic rotors (16.5-inch up front and 16.1-inch at the rear) that bite hard. The pedal doesn’t feel as wooden as the Lambo’s, where more force yields more stopping power. In the Nuvolari, a spring change within the brake actuator feels like it prioritizes pedal travel to modulate the brakes rather than pressure. Nevertheless, the pedal feels great.

See all results for new 2028 Audi Nuvolari for sale near 22206

Bending the Nuvolari into Turn 2 reveals off-center steering feel that isn’t nearly as over-caffeinated as the Lamborghini’s. Here, it feels very Audi. Effort ramps up in a linear fashion but is never too heavy. It’s as direct as it needs to be, and there’s ample indication when the front tires have had enough.

A nearly 1000-hp supercar should be somewhat intimidating to drive, but Audi has tuned the Nuvolari to be a gentle beast. Audi’s Quattro Predictive Drive system uses a 6-D sensor (as in the Revuelto SV) to absorb information from the car, and, based on driving habits, in-house-developed algorithms predict what the car should do next. Tail out on corner exit? The car’s computer brain might send a little extra torque vectoring to the front axle to keep things in check. Crank a little too much steering input into a large braking event? You can feel the motors straighten out the car.

The Predictive Drive system also communicates with the dampers. They’re adaptive units with high- and low-speed electronic controls for the compression and rebound sides. The dampers allow Audi to use a softer spring than the Temerario to help maintain a consistent tire patch and keep the car stable during braking and the body flat when the Bridgestone Potenza Race tires are loaded up midcorner.

With Predictive Drive working in the background, the rest of our extremely limited time in the Nuvolari is spent trying to digest the experience. Don’t forget to tug the massive aluminum shift paddles before slamming into the 10,000-rpm limiter. Check. What’s after this corner? I can’t remember; Victor said something about braking. Speaking of braking, is the rear motor really braking the engine when there’s more horsepower than is available for traction to harvest extra energy for the front straight? There’s no indication it’s happening, but we’ll take their word for it.

Familiarizing yourself with your very own Nuvolari will cost north of $700,000. That’s before customizing one of the 499 Nuvolaris that will be built. You can specify any color you’d like or choose an unpainted carbon-fiber body for an unspecified cost, something we’re excited to see. We’re even more excited to see how Audi’s return to the supercar world trickles down into the RS brand. We’ll be waiting.

#4452. The Mercedes-Benz EQS drove 539 miles on a single charge. Still worried about range?

The new Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ covered 539 miles without stopping to charge, making range anxiety look like a thing of the past.

Mercedes-Benz overhauled the EQS electric sedan, including a bigger battery and an 800V electrical architecture.

The 2027 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ uses a 122 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 467 miles.

While that’s already impressive, the electric sedan will likely go even farther in everyday driving conditions. During Edmunds recent EV Range Test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ drove a whopping 539 miles without stopping to charge.

The EQS beat its own EPA estimate by 72 miles and is now the longest-range electric sedan Edmunds has ever tested, beating the Lucid Air, the first EV to break the 500-mile mark. The only EV that has it beat is the Cadillac Escalade IQ, which managed 558 miles from its massive 205 kWh battery.

During the test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ was also more efficient than its official numbers suggest.

The new EQS used 29.6 kWh per 100 miles, beating its EPA estimate of 28 kWh per 100 miles. In comparison, the 2025 Mercedes EQS 450+ covered 464 miles and used 34 kWh per 100 miles during the same test, so the improvements are considerable.

Edmunds observed a peak charging rate of 350 kW, in line with Mercedes’ estimates, while it sustained an average of 222 kW throughout the session.

Both beat the older EQS, which reached a peak charge rate of 208 kW and sustained an average of 175 kW.

The new Mercedes EQS 450+ added 825 miles of range in an hour, and 100 miles in just over 7 minutes, nearly twice the speed of the 2025MY.

The Edmunds EV Range Test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions. It includes 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set to auto at 72 degrees.

How much is too much? 539 miles on a single charge is impressive, but do you need it? In a recent “nationally representative” survey, BMW found that Americans want more EV range than they actually need.

The study showed that 73% consider 25, 50, or 75 miles enough to cover their daily driving. However, 42% said they would require at least 300 miles of range before they would consider an EV.

If you have access to a home charger, nothing beats waking up with a full charge every day. Meanwhile, public charging continues to improve, giving EV drivers more reliable options on longer trips.

Faster charging also helps. Another 53% said they would be more likely to consider an EV if it could add about 150 miles of range in around 10 minutes.

In the same Edmunds EV Range Test last week, the new 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive drove 436 miles on a single charge, exceeding its EPA estimate of 392 miles by 44 miles. It also used 28.3 kWh per 100 miles during the test, beating its official EPA estimate of 32 kWh per 100 miles.

I'm really glad to see more articles like this and people talking more about efficiency. It's not just about bigger batteries and range. It needs to be about smaller batteries plus great efficiency giving that same range. We need to do this with more efficient designs, more sedans and lighter vehicles.

The new 2027 Volvo EX60 drove 352 miles while the 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric covered 392 miles during the same test.

One thing is certain: electric vehicles are becoming more efficient, enabling longer driving ranges and faster charging times. As battery tech advances, EVs will drive farther and charge faster, while safety and performance will continue to improve.

How much driving range would you consider enough for your daily drive? What about for the week? Let us know in the comments below.

#4451. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

#4449. PlugShare finally adds dark mode, and there’s more for EV drivers

PlugShare is giving its EV charging app a big overhaul. Version 8.0 arrives worldwide for iPhone on November 10, with dark mode, a trip planner that shows how far apart charging stops are, and a rebuilt Apple Watch app that can point you to a charger compatible with your EV.

Dark mode was one of the most-requested features from PlugShare users. It works across the app and follows your iPhone’s settings, so if your phone switches to dark mode at sunset, your charging map will, too.

The trip planner gets a small but handy change. Each charging stop now shows how far it is from both the start of your trip and the previous stop. So when you’re deciding whether to stretch to the next fast charger or stop sooner, the number you need is right there.

PlugShare now loads your saved locations, trips, and profile when you open the app or sign in, so those tabs are ready to tap. You can also open and zoom in on station photos right from their thumbnails. That’s handy when you’re trying to figure out what corner a charging station is in in a big parking lot. The app also adapts its layout to the iPhone Duo’s different screens and folded positions.

The rebuilt Watch app lists nearby charging stations with distances and directions. It uses the filters you’ve set on your iPhone, so if you’ve filtered for plugs that fit your EV, that carries over to your wrist.

Tap a station and you’ll see its PlugScore, the network that runs it, a small map, and which plugs it has, including NACS, CCS, CHAdeMO, or J1772. The list refreshes when you raise your wrist and open the app. You can also add a shortcut to a round or corner slot on your watch face.

The iPhone update is rolling out through the App Store. PlugShare says Android users will get dark mode and a redesign based on Google’s Material 3 in early 2027.

#4448. Nissan Brings Back the Patrol Name on the 2027 Armada Pro-4X

For the first time since 1969, Nissan will sell a vehicle with the Patrol name in the United States, adding the iconic moniker to the Armada Pro-4X.

There’s a small but significant change coming to the Nissan Armada for 2027. Since the second-generation launched in 2017, the full-size SUV has essentially been a rebadged version of the Patrol SUV sold overseas. Now, the Patrol nameplate will no longer be forbidden fruit. For the 2027 model year, the Armada’s off-road trim has officially been renamed the Armada Patrol Pro-4X.

This is the first time the Patrol nameplate has appeared stateside since 1969, when the second-generation Patrol was offered via Datsun dealerships as the first Nissan-badged vehicle in the U.S. The move to bring back the Patrol name in the U.S. aligns with the off-roader’s 75th anniversary, with production first kicking off in 1951.

See all results for new 2027 Nissan Armada for sale near 94043

The newly renamed model wears a Patrol badge across the rear end, while Armada is printed on the D-pillar. Inside, there are badges that say “Patrol” and “Since 1951” on the center console. The Armada Patrol Pro-4X also adds some new optional equipment, including new NISMO rock sliders and a NISMO roof rack. There are also new NISMO Axis wheels wrapped in BFGoodrich all-terrain tires available for 2027.

Otherwise, the Pro-4X carries over unchanged, still packing an electronic locking rear differential, adaptive air suspension, and a metal underbody skid plate. Under the hood, the twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V-6 remains, still putting out 425 horsepower to all four wheels.

Production of the renamed Armada Patrol Pro-4X begins in November and will be shown for the first time at the 2026 Los Angeles auto show later this month. The Armada Patrol Pro-4X will start at $81,265, a significant increase from last year when it cost $76,575. However, the Pro-4X now comes standard with the Premium package, which cost $2780 for the 2026 model year and brought goodies like a panoramic sunroof, heated second-row seats, a power liftgate, and 12-way power front seats with heating and ventilation. That means the 2027 Pro-4X is only $1910 more than a Pro-4X with the Premium package from last year.

#4447. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4445. Humble Hauler autonomous trailer takes the truck out of trucking [update]

Less than a year after its founding, truckless trucking brand Humble Robotics has secured more than $75 million after a $51 million Series A funding round that will fuel the company’s transition from prototype to preproduction.

The latest funding round for the driverless, cab-less, and truck-less battery-electric freight platform developer was led by Obvious Ventures with participation from other existing investors Eclipse and Energy Impact Partners. Humble said it will use the funding for customer pilots, testing and validation, and early manufacturing.

“We’ve spent years proving that a truck can drive itself,” explains Humble Robotics founder and CEO, Eyal Cohen. “The harder question is how to make autonomy something a freight operator can depend on every day.”

We originally covered the Humble Hauler back in May. You can check out the original article, below, then let us know what you think of the company’s prospects in the comments.

The startup that dares to ask, “Why does the Macbook driving my freight around need a whole cab?” just showed off a fully driverless, cab-less, and truck-less battery-electric freight platform designed to handle containerized cargo more efficiently than ever.

Instead of looking at the tractor and asking how to make it work without a driver, Humble looked at the trailer, itself, redesigning the container chassis as a vehicle from the ground up. The end result isn’t just an autonomous solution, it’s an overall lighter platform without a cab that saves shippers the weight of a sleeper cab, a day cab, or the truck at all.

The Humble approach is said to improve payload efficiency of shipping containers, and intended for dock-to-dock operation.

“I have dedicated my career to building electric and autonomous vehicle technology,” explains Eyal Cohen, Humble Robotics’ founder and CEO. “For the first time, freight can be fully automated all the way to the loading dock. We are making freight sustainable, safe and efficient in a way no one thought was possible. And we’re doing it with an exceptional team of industry veterans and AV experts.”

Emerging from stealth after a $24 million funding round, Humble claims to have completed its first Humble Hauler prototype in less than six months – and they’ll soon be ready to begin autonomous testing in pilot programs with a number of logistics partners.

The vehicle uses a combination of cameras, lidar, and radar for 360-degree awareness (unhindered by seeing around a cab), and uses vision-language-action models to help the system respond to new scenarios.

Thanks to superior battery tech, a maturing global charging infrastructure, and a permanently damaged MidEast oil supply, there’s never been a better time to be an EV startup. Humble is hitting all the electric trailer buzzwords, too, while also touting the fact that the electric powertrain can reduce a company’s to volatile fuel prices even as it helps produce other cost benefits like lower maintenance costs.

There is a reason why the transportation industry developed separate cabs and trailers. Trailers can be loaded or unloaded for days and are much less expensive than trucks that serve both purposes in one piece. That allows the more expensive piece of the transport puzzle to be used more and allows the trailer to be loaded and unloaded while the cab is elsewhere working or in the shop. Query whether the savings they cite will surpass the costs of not having the flexibility of a cab and trailer design.

And if a robot like this can deliver on its promises without the baked-in inefficiencies of humanoids, they might be one step closer to provide that the most efficient solution to a problem is rarely a general one, and even rarer is it a solution that looks like a human.

#4444. Battlefield 6 Loses Court Case Over Ban

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Account bans are a dangerous thing, especially for titles with a price tag. There’s a reason most games make you agree to terms of use before you get started playing online, clarifying bannable offenses and ensuring you know the groundwork you’re playing under. Without them, and without proper explanations for bans, companies can get into more than just PR trouble.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

Back in early August, a Battlefield 6 player named Rychadv complained on Reddit that his profile has been randomly, unexplainably banned after a period of inactivity, with no support levied from EA after attempts at appeal. Today, he revealed that he took EA to court over the case and won, regaining access to his account effective immediately.

While most don’t carefully read the terms and conditions many online games ask of you, the agreement does serve as somewhat legally binding, acting as a way for the studio running the game to establish when and if they can pull your plug. Cheating, improper communications use, or any step out of line with the terms laid out can be used as a justification to temporarily, or permanently, ban you.

The odd part that swung this case fully in Rychadv’s favor was the lack of an actual motive. For no discernible reason, after an extended break from the game, DICE had simply banned his account, with no means of reacquiring it or fighting the ban. Especially on a full-priced title like Battlefield 6, this type of hiccup is strictly unacceptable, potentially costing Rychadv a whole new copy if he didn’t drag DICE to court.

Bans need to be carefully considered by studios before they’re implemented; otherwise, they risk both stepping on toes and unjustly kicking out solid chunks of their populace. The threat of bans, more so than the bans themselves, is often enough to keep the problem children in line. We’ve all had a mouthy, rude player on the team, the more invested in the game they are, the less likely they are to get heinous.

Without them, and without proper explanations for bans, companies can get into more than just PR trouble.

This widely depends on both the player culture and ban frequency of the game itself, and is far more common in free-to-play titles where accounts can quickly rise and fall. For full-priced experiences, developers need to be a bit more careful with the ban hammer, and they especially need to make sure any perceived bannable offenses actually happened.

The gradual move away from physical media for the majority of the gaming industry makes the threat of random bans a bit more serious, especially with cases like Rychadv’s still out in the open. It’s not just multiplayer titles that are always online, and who's to say some studio couldn’t kick you out for what you do in a single-player game in the future, even when it's only affecting your copy?

This is definitely stepping into the speculative, but it's important to remember that digital titles aren’t really yours; you simply buy a license from the studio to play. Without the promise of physical media, there’s a certain formlessness to the games we buy, like they could slip away at any moment.

With no promise of actual ownership, situations like Rychadv’s could happen more and more, putting the onus of action onto the players to hold studios over the fire a bit. When you agree to the terms of service, make sure to read up on it. While you’re playing by the studio’s rules, they need to respect them as well, especially for titles with a price tag.

Improper use of bans could lead to more legal disputes like Rychadv’s, as players become more willing to hold studios to their word.

Deadlock is starting to suffer from the same fate as other free-to-play games, with bot farmers crawling from the woodwork.

#4443. Subcompact SUVs May Seem Appealing, but Compact Cars Are Often a Better Buy

Unless you’re dead set on the tall seating position that an SUV provides, we think these small hatchbacks are far more satisfying than their crossover siblings.

Sure, SUVs are popular, but that doesn’t mean they’re always the best choice for your needs. The smaller an SUV gets, the fewer advantages it offers when compared with an equivalent sedan or hatchback. Here, we’re looking at the subcompact SUV segment and stacking up these small crossovers against compact cars from the same brand.

Subcompact SUVs are the smallest of their species. As the name suggests, they’re smaller than compact SUVs, and their tidier footprints often mean compromises in space, fuel economy, and driving satisfaction.

Automakers feel the need to offer additional ground clearance and all-wheel drive in these SUV models to justify their categorization. But these models typically share the same underpinnings and engines as their compact-car kin.

This means these SUV models are often heavier, less enjoyable to drive, and less fuel-efficient than their non-SUV siblings. Both types of vehicles also typically offer similar amounts of cargo and passenger space. Pricing, meanwhile, tends to favor the compact hatchbacks.

If these two types of vehicles are so similar, then why the different classifications? Blame size creep.

Cars and SUVs typically get larger with each passing generation. Let’s roll the clock back 25 years. While most modern compact cars are bigger than their counterparts from a quarter century ago, they still tend to cast smaller shadows than mid-size cars from the turn of the millennium.

On the other hand, the subcompact SUVs of today are typically larger than the compact SUVs of 25 years ago. Due to this, calling a modern SUV “subcompact” better describes its size relative to the overall SUV landscape as opposed to the larger passenger-vehicle space.

Odds are that if you’re shopping for one of these small-sized SUVs, you’re going to be just as well—if not better—served by these vehicles’ often less expensive and more fun-to-drive compact hatchback stablemates.

The HR-V is Honda's smallest SUV, but it’s still plenty spacious inside. The main downside of this model is that it’s available with only one powertrain: a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter inline-four that produces just 158 horsepower.

This means the HR-V accelerates at a leisurely pace. In our testing, this little Honda SUV needed 9.4 seconds to hit 60 mph.

The HR-V earns an EPA-estimated combined rating of 28 mpg in front-drive form. Adding all-wheel drive drops that figure to 27 mpg.

The Honda Civic hatchback has the same base engine as the CR-V, but it also offers a more powerful and more fuel-efficient hybrid variant that has quicker acceleration and much better fuel economy—up to 49 mpg combined, according to the EPA. The Civic doesn’t offer all-wheel drive as the HR-V does, but we’d advocate for a good set of winter tires instead.

In our testing, the Civic hatchback’s cargo area was only marginally smaller than the HR-V’s. It held six carry-on suitcases behind the rear seat, which is only one fewer case than the HR-V can accommodate.

More importantly, the Civic is far more fun to drive than the HR-V.

The Subaru Crosstrek is the spiritual successor to the old Impreza Outback Sport, which was essentially an Impreza hatchback with added body cladding. Compared to the old Outback Sport, the Crosstrek is a bit more distinct than the Impreza it’s based on. Even so, the Crosstrek is still effectively a lifted Impreza hatch with additional ground clearance and more rugged looks. As such, we don’t think the Crosstrek is worth the extra cost over the run-of-the-mill Impreza hatchback that Subaru still offers.

Subaru makes an even better case for the Impreza hatch for 2027 courtesy of a new base model that starts at less than $26,000. As we previously detailed, the Impreza beats the Crosstrek in nearly every metric in our testing: It’s quicker, more fuel-efficient, and offers as much space inside. The only reason we can think of to choose the Crosstrek is for its available gas-electric hybrid powertrain or its extra ground clearance.

A redesign for 2027 brings eye-catching new looks to the Kia Seltos subcompact SUV. A 147-hp four-cylinder comes standard, while a 190-hp turbo four is optional. For its second generation, the Seltos also offers an available gas-electric hybrid powertrain—an option the Kia K4 compact hatch lacks.

Sure, the Kia K4 hatchback doesn’t offer hybrid power. However, what this handsome hatch lacks in powertrain options, it makes up for in other ways.

Simply put, we prefer the way the K4 drives to the Seltos. Credit the compact hatchback’s lower center of gravity, which improves handling and behind-the-wheel engagement.

The K4 is also more miserly than the equivalent gas-only Seltos. When fitted with the available 190-hp turbocharged 1.6-liter four-cylinder, the K4 hatch is also notably quicker than its equally powerful Seltos kin. In our testing, a so-equipped K4 hatch accelerated to 60 mph in 7.0 seconds, while a turbocharged Seltos needed 8.2 seconds to hit the same mark.

We haven’t yet measured how many carry-on suitcases fit in the cargo bay of the new Seltos. Compared to the previous-generation Seltos, though, the K4 hatch fell one carry-on suitcase short of its subcompact SUV sibling’s sum.

The Mazda CX-30 is among our favorite subcompact crossover SUVs. It drives great, features a high-quality interior, and provides sufficient oomph with the standard 186-hp 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine. Opt for the 250-hp turbocharged 2.5-liter, and the all-wheel-drive CX-30 accelerates with even more vigor. But what if Mazda also sold a vehicle that paired all the positive traits of the CX-30 with a lower starting price, even better driving dynamics, and an available manual gearbox? Well, good news: It does.

The Mazda 3 hatchback may do without the higher seating position of the CX-30, but it makes up for it with livelier dynamics courtesy of its lower center of gravity and lighter curb weight. At a manufacturer-estimated 3111 pounds, the front-drive 3 hatch’s mass undercuts that of the all-wheel-drive CX-30 by 284 pounds.

While we think the available six-speed manual gearbox of the front-drive 3 makes it superior to its all-wheel-drive kin, we know not everyone will agree with us. No worries, though, because Mazda also offers the 3 with all-wheel drive. Opting for it adds 172 pounds to the curb weight of 3 hatchbacks with the standard 186-hp four. However, AWD is standard on turbocharged models.

In our testing, both the 3 hatchback and CX-30 were able to hold up to 16 carry-on suitcases with the rear seats folded. With the rear seats in place, the 3 hatch’s cargo area held five carry-on suitcases—just one fewer than the CX-30.

Acura’s subcompact SUV is about as interesting and exciting as watching C-SPAN. Short of its available all-wheel-drive system and slightly bigger interior compartment, there are few other reasons to pick the ADX over its compact hatchback sibling, the Integra.

With a starting price of $34,795, the Acura Integra undercuts the ADX by a significant $1755. It’s also significantly more enjoyable to drive and a good deal quicker.

Though both the Integra and ADX come standard with a turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine that mates to a continuously variable automatic transmission (CVT), the Integra benefits from an extra 10 horsepower and 13 pound-feet of torque relative to the unit in the ADX. With 200 horsepower and 192 pound-feet of torque, a CVT-equipped Integra accelerated to 60 mph in a reasonable 7.1 seconds. An all-wheel-drive ADX, meanwhile, required a languid 8.7 ticks to hit 60 mph.

Admittedly, the fastback shape of the Integra cuts into its cargo-carrying capabilities. We fit 18 carry-on suitcases in its cargo bay with the rear seats folded and five with the seatbacks up. The squarer shape of the ADX afforded totals of 22 and seven, respectively.

Despite being raised on a steady diet of base-model Hondas and Toyotas—or perhaps because of it—Joey Capparella cultivated an obsession for the automotive industry throughout his childhood in Nashville, Tennessee. He found a way to write about cars for the school newspaper during his college years at Rice University, which eventually led him to move to Ann Arbor, Michigan, for his first professional auto-writing gig at Automobile Magazine. His previous experience includes stints as an editor at publications such as U.S. News & World Report, The Huffington Post, Motor1.com, and MotorTrend.

#4442. Honda shows off its next electric motorcycle, and it’s wilder than you thought

Honda has been getting increasingly serious about electric motorcycles, but if you want to see just how weird the company thinks the future could get, take a look at the Honda EV Outlier Concept.

I got a chance to see the wild-looking machine in person at EICMA in Milan, where it looked like almost nothing else on the show floor. And that’s exactly the point.

The EV Outlier Concept originally debuted at last year’s Japan Mobility Show as Honda’s attempt to imagine an electric motorcycle that isn’t simply a conventional motorcycle with the engine swapped for a battery and motor. In fact, Honda describes the concept as looking toward the future of electric motorcycles beyond 2030.

Instead of a centrally mounted motor driving the rear wheel, the EV Outlier uses motors inside both wheels, giving it all-wheel drive and allowing Honda’s designers to completely rethink the rest of the motorcycle’s layout. The battery is housed in that large central black body, while the rider sits extremely low and behind it.

Honda describes the design philosophy with three words: “Gliding, Ecstasy, and Low.” The first refers to the smooth, nearly silent feeling of electric propulsion, while the second describes the instant acceleration and massive torque available from independently controlled front and rear motors. “Low” is more literal: Honda deliberately dropped the rider’s seating and eye position to create an entirely different sensation from a conventional motorcycle.

There’s even a bucket-style backrest designed to support the rider under hard acceleration and let the rider pivot through corners around their hips.

Up front, traditional mirrors are replaced by cameras, while a wide digital cockpit can display things like lean angle, riding modes, front motor torque adjustment, and what the two wheels are doing in real time.

Will Honda actually build this thing? Almost certainly not exactly as you see it here. That’s what concepts are for.

But the EV Outlier is still interesting as a statement of intent. Honda is obviously still playing around with the freedom that electric drivetrains offer, and the company is asking what motorcycles could become once designers no longer have to work around engines, fuel tanks, transmissions, and traditional drivetrains.

And judging by what I saw at EICMA, Honda’s answer could get pretty wild.

#4441. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

It looks like it's going to take the Arc Raiders community a bit of work to unlock the game's next map.

As many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

The event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

The new model will likely drop the Shelby name, and it’s expected to be naturally aspirated and fall between the Dark Horse and Dark Horse SC.

Now that Ford finally has a Porsche 911 GT3 RS competitor in the Mustang GTD, it seems that the company wants to adopt a bit more from the folks over in Stuttgart. Porsche has become famous for splitting hairs with the 911 lineup by offering seemingly endless variants of the same model. Now, according to a new report from Ford Authority, the Ford Motor Company is planning to expand the Mustang lineup even further with the launch of a spiritual successor to the Mustang Shelby GT350.

Amid the EcoBoost, GT, Dark Horse, Dark Horse SC, and GTD, a GT350 successor would be the sixth Mustang on offer. And that figure doesn’t include any of the Premium or convertible variants.

Rather than utilizing the supercharged 5.2-liter V-8 found in the SC, Ford is expected to give the GT350 successor a naturally aspirated mill. #4438. CAT puts century-old train tech to work in its biggest underground machine yet

Diesel-electric locomotives have been barreling along America’s wide-open spaces for generations, and the century-old combination of highly efficient diesel engines spinning up generators to power high-torque electric motors has proven tough to beat. Now, Caterpillar is putting that century-old concept to work underground. Meet the CAT R3200 XE LHD.

One of the many hard-working machines moving chunks of Earth under your feet, an LHD (load, haul, and dump) machine is essentially a massive underground wheel loader designed to scoop up blasted rock, haul it through narrow mine tunnels, then dump it into trucks or ore passes. Built low and wide to fit in the tunnels, LHDs are workhorses of underground mining operations – and the new R3200 XE is CAT’s biggest yet, with a 25 ton payload and electric drive.

Before we get into the machine’s specs (the few that we have, anyway), I want to make sure understand that large-scale mining operations use obscene amounts of fuel, and a swing in site efficiency of just 1-2% can mean a huge difference in the bottom line – and fuel prices were up 27.4% (!) in August alone.

Keep the staggering weight of what that kind of fuel cost can mean to a fleet that buys fuel by the literal truckload as you read the rest of this.

Though not yet officially released by CAT, snippets of the company’s launch video have been leaking through dealers and trade journals, and they show the big machine powered by CAT’s newest 18.1 liter Tier 5 C18 diesel generator making 527 hp (~390 kW). That C18 reportedly sends electrons to the same electric drive system used in the company’s already successful 18-ton R2900 XE LHD.

In addition to a bigger generator and heftier payload, CAT says the upcoming R3200 XE LHD offers reduced cycle times versus the R2900 XE with 11% better speed on grade, plus reduced maintenance and repair costs thanks to design refinements for better durability, including redesigned axle. All told, that works out to 28% more tons per hour with 8% better fuel efficiency.

That efficiency is boosted by the same baked-in ADAS tech that’s made the smaller R2900 XE a favorite, and includes the latest version of CAT AutoDig and MineStar, ensuring that the machines are easy for experienced CAT operators to set up for remote, semi-autonomous, and even fully autonomous operation using Command for Underground.

We’ll post an update once CAT makes the full rundown of official specs public, which should be sooner rather than later. When that happens, we’ll see exactly how this big burrowing CAT stacks up against the competition from Sandvik, Epiroc, and Komatsu. In the meantime, let us know what you think of CAT’s newest electric drive machine in the comments.

#4436. Honda Announces Plans to Build a New $3 Billion Factory in Ohio

The new factory will be Honda’s third in Ohio, and Honda is also investing in its transmission facilities to convert them to building hybrid systems.

Honda is already well entrenched in Ohio. The Japanese automaker has two vehicle assembly factories in the state, in East Liberty and Marysville, along with the Anna Engine Plant and a transmission facility in Russells Point. Now Honda is taking its commitment to Ohio even further, announcing today a plant to build a new factory in Central Ohio and to invest $3 billion into the project.

The new factory will be located near Honda’s existing manufacturing facilities, on land between the East Liberty and Marysville plants. Production is set to kick off in 2029, and the factory will have a planned capacity of 240,000 vehicles, boosting Honda’s U.S. production capacity to around 1.3 million vehicles per year. The new factory will create over 2000 new jobs, Honda says. Honda didn’t specify what would be built at the new factory but did say it would be capable of producing everything from gas-powered models to hybrids and full EVs.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 94043

The new factory is just one part of an increased investment in hybrid vehicles from Honda. The company is also investing in its factory in Lincoln, Alabama, planning to increase production capacity and expand engine production to include a new V-6 hybrid powertrain. Honda says the plant will also get more flexible, by being able to build multiple models on the two vehicle production lines. The Anna Engine Plant, meanwhile, is undergoing a substantial retooling in order to produce a next-generation Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder engine for upcoming compact and midsize models.

Honda’s transmission factory in Ohio is also getting retooled, with an existing transmission production line set to become a second production line for next-generation hybrid systems bound for compact and midsize vehicles. The facility will also lead the way on Honda’s hybrid system for larger vehicles, which will also be produced at Honda’s transmission factory in Georgia. More details on the vehicles that will use these new hybrid systems should emerge over the next couple of years.

Boolok, a Support Agent-affiliated Physical damage dealing Bangboo bringing a giant block hammer to the fight to, well, smash enemies with.

It’s a bit of a winter party in Version 2.4, it seems, as the update will bring back Hugo (Attack - Ice), and Ellen (Attack - Ice), too.

#4434. Polestar unveils Formula 2030 concept, previewing the next Polestar 2

Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.

The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.

We reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg. Now we get the full set of pictures and the details.

It’s the first show car built under head of design Philipp Römers, who joined from Audi in 2024.

Polestar calls the Formula 2030 a “compact practical four-door sports car” that “sits within its own segment.” It’s 4,680 mm (184.3 inches) long and 2,021 mm (79.6 inches) wide, on a 2,780 mm (109.4-inch) wheelbase.

For context, that’s about 3 inches longer than today’s Polestar 2 and roughly 5 inches lower. It’s also a bit shorter than a Tesla Model 3 and sits 3.5 inches closer to the ground. Polestar says the concept lands “somewhere between” the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 in size.

The proportions are classic sports car: long hood, short overhangs, the cabin pushed back over big rear haunches, and 22-inch center-lock wheels. There are gold Brembo calipers behind those wheels and Öhlins dampers on display in the trunk.

Up front, Polestar kept its “Dual Blade” headlights, now set into an aero wing over a shark nose and a deep splitter. The automaker says this is the face of the next-generation Polestar 2 planned for 2027.

There’s a single vertical windshield wiper, like on a race car, and a LiDAR unit that hides under an aerodynamic shroud and only shows itself when the car is driving autonomously.

The rear is where things change the most. Polestar dropped the full-width light bar, which is on just about every EV these days, for what it calls “Single Blade” rear lights. It says they are being introduced here “ahead of series production.”

Römers described the concept as a “bold evolution” of the brand’s existing design:

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

The rear doors are hinged at the back and there’s no B-pillar, so the whole side opens up to four individual seats.

The interior is built around the driver. A curved 20-inch display, which Polestar calls the “HyperDIM,” is mounted directly on the steering column, and a 12.2-inch center screen sits in the center tunnel.

But the bigger news is below that screen. Polestar added a panel of eight physical controls for the most-used functions, and owners could swap between types of controls, like rocker switches or rotary knobs, and program what each one does.

Polestar says it is “committing to rebalance the mix of physical and digital.” Juan Pablo Bernal, the company’s head of interior design, put it plainly:

“As a performance brand, we see a renewed focus on the driver, and so we re-balance the digital and physical. We introduce physical buttons and controls.”

That’s a big change for a brand whose recent cars run almost everything through the center touchscreen.

The cabin also physically changes with the drive mode. There are three of them: Performance, Normal, and Autonomous. In Performance, the center screen drops flush into the console and the steering wheel and its display pull closer to the driver. In Autonomous, the wheel and the seat move away from each other.

The four seats use inflatable bolsters that shape themselves to each occupant, and the seat backs are made of a flax-based composite instead of virgin plastic. Google Gemini is built in, like in Polestar’s production cars.

The cargo area is the strangest part of the car. The rear opens as a clamshell, and the trunk floor is transparent, with custom Polestar bags strapped down underneath it with gold straps.

Up front, the frunk holds two race helmets and a fire extinguisher, framed by a gold strut brace.

Now for what’s missing. Polestar didn’t release a single powertrain spec. No battery size, no range, no power output, and no price. This is a design study, and Polestar isn’t saying it will build it.

What it does say is that “various design attributes” from the concept will show up on the next Polestar 2 in 2027 and the Polestar 7 in 2028. Those are two of the four new models Polestar plans to launch in three years, and the 7 is going to be built in Europe.

Europe is where this matters, since Polestar is shut out of the US under the federal connected-vehicle rule. The concept made its debut during the media drive of the Polestar 4 SUV.

Polestar always impresses me with its design, and this is no exception with this new head of design.

The proportions are sharp. Long hood, cabin pushed back, big haunches, and a roofline lower than the Polestar 5’s on a car with four doors and four real seats. If the next Polestar 2 keeps even half of this stance, it’s going to be the best-looking car in its segment.

I don’t know about the trunk of this thing. Polestar itself calls the rear “UFO-esque,” and between the wraparound glass, the clamshell and the see-through floor, it’s a lot. But everything else on this car is pretty sharp.

Polestar is putting physical controls back in its cars and saying so in plain words. The way they talk about it makes it sound like you can expect that of upcoming production vehicles.

Now the usual caveat. A concept car doesn’t fix a balance sheet. Polestar lost $842 million in the first half of this year on a negative gross margin. Design has never been Polestar’s problem. Building these cars and selling them at a profit is.
